paragraphs: ## Node 01 · The Contact — Buga, Valle del Cauca

Lucho [[pperf|had never lived|Past perfect (never … before)]] far from home before. At twenty-five, with a diploma in electrical engineering and a small suitcase, he [[psimp|arrived]] in Buga to start his second job. During his first weeks he [[pcont|was always measuring|Past continuous (repeated background action)]] voltages and inspecting panels. Then, at work, he [[psimp|met]] Carolina.

She [[psimp|was]] forty-five and divorced, and nothing seemed to surprise her. Lucho [[pperf|had spent|Past perfect (before the story)]] his teenage years with books, not with people, so he [[psimp|found]] her fascinating. “You're very young,” she [[psimp|said]] that first afternoon. “I'm twenty-five,” he [[psimp|answered]]. She [[psimp|laughed]], and something inside him [[psimp|closed]], like a switch.
## Node 02 · No Reference — The first three months

Nobody at the office knew it, but Lucho [[pperf|had never had]] a girlfriend. While other young men [[pcont|were learning|Past continuous (while + action in progress)]] how to argue and forgive, he [[pcont|was studying]] how electric current behaves. So he [[psimp|had]] no reference.

Within three months he [[psimp|was]] in love. If she [[psimp|called]], he [[psimp|answered]]. If she [[psimp|was]] sad, he [[psimp|cancelled]] his plans. Carolina [[psimp|lived]] with her seventeen-year-old son in a house that really belonged to the bank. She [[psimp|had]] a mortgage, a car loan and three credit cards. “If I only pay the minimum, I'll never finish,” she [[psimp|told]] him once, laughing.
## Node 03 · Heat, Then Fire — Year one

Her whims [[psimp|started]] small: a dinner here, a weekend there, a new phone. Lucho [[psimp|paid]], and paying [[psimp|felt]] like proof of love. By the end of the first year, he [[pperf|had asked|Past perfect (By the end of … + had)]] for two advances on his salary, and the bank [[pperf|had raised]] his credit limit twice. He [[pcont|was paying]] for her expenses as well as his own. He never [[psimp|called]] it debt. He [[psimp|called]] it helping.

There is a rule in electrical work: resistance produces heat, and heat produces fire. Lucho [[pperf|had explained]] it to technicians dozens of times, but he [[psimp|couldn't]] apply it to his own life.
## Node 04 · The Lights Go Out Quietly — Manizales, Caldas

His parents [[pcont|were waiting]] for him in Manizales. At first he [[used|used to visit|used to + infinitive (past habit)]] them every month; then every two months; then he [[psimp|stopped]] counting. Weekends [[psimp|were]] expensive, and Carolina [[psimp|needed]] him. His mother [[used|used to phone]] every Sunday, but he [[psimp|answered]] less and less. When Lucho finally [[psimp|noticed]], more than a year [[pperf|had passed|Past perfect (when + past simple, had + participle)]] without a single visit.
An open circuit is not dramatic. Nothing explodes. The current simply stops arriving, and everything goes dark, quietly.
## Node 05 · What Distance Removes — Ibagué, Tolima

After almost two years, his company [[psimp|transferred]] Lucho to Ibagué. For two years he [[pperf|had organised]] his life around her moods and her emergencies, so he [[pperf|had almost forgotten]] how to spend a Sunday alone. Every night he [[pcont|was working]] late, calling her at eleven and counting the days. In the silence, Lucho [[psimp|heard]] the truth about the relationship, but he [[psimp|didn't want]] to say it.
## Node 06 · The Invoice — A Tuesday, over the phone

In the end, Carolina [[psimp|ended]] it. She [[psimp|called]] him one Tuesday while he [[pcont|was having|Past continuous interrupted by past simple]] dinner. She [[psimp|said]] she needed her freedom and that he deserved somebody his own age. As soon as she [[pperf|had finished]], he [[psimp|apologised]] — but he [[psimp|didn't know]] why.

He [[psimp|hung]] up. Two years, a higher credit limit and a family he [[pperf|had stopped]] visiting: that was the invoice. He [[psimp|felt]] like a house at three in the morning, with everything switched off.
## Node 07 · A Second Circuit — Ibagué · a few weeks later

A few weeks later he [[pcont|was going out]] with Silvia, a twenty-two-year-old girl who laughed easily. With Carolina he [[used|used to remember]] every small detail. But he [[pperf|had left]] something behind in Buga: the patience, the small attentions, the crazy devotion. He [[psimp|was]] affectionate, but in an efficient way.

Silvia [[psimp|noticed]]. She [[pperf|had never met]] Carolina, but she could feel her. “You treat me like an obligation,” she [[psimp|told]] him. “That's not true,” he [[psimp|said]], and [[psimp|changed]] the subject. She has threatened to leave him five times, but she has never packed a bag.

Then one night she [[psimp|told]] him a secret that she [[pperf|had kept]] for weeks: her ex-boyfriend [[pperf|had come]] to her house once. Nothing [[pperf|had happened]], she said. title: Short Circuit · C1
focus: Inversion, cleft sentences, participle clauses and advanced vocabulary
advisory: Tema adulto: una relación de pareja desigual, deudas y distancia familiar. Recomendada para jóvenes y adultos.
paragraphs: ## Node 01 · The Contact — Buga, Valle del Cauca

[[inv|Never before had Lucho lived|Negative adverbial inversion (Never before + had + subject)]] more than a bus ride away from his parents. At twenty-five, [[part|armed with a diploma in electrical engineering and a suitcase hopelessly inadequate for two years|Past participle clause (armed with …)]], he arrived in Buga to take up his second post.

The town received him the way small towns receive outsiders: [[voc|courteously|C1 vocabulary: politely, with good manners]], and without haste. [[part|Measuring voltages, inspecting panels and memorising streets that all seemed to converge on the same church|Present participle clause (-ing, simultaneous actions)]], he barely noticed his first weeks slip by. [[inv|Had anyone suggested that the most hazardous circuit in Buga lay outside any building, he would have laughed it off.|Inverted third conditional (Had + subject + past participle)]]
[[cleft|It was at work, of all places, that he met Carolina.|It-cleft (It was … that) for emphasis]]

She was forty-five, divorced, and [[adv|moved through the world as though nothing could catch her off guard any longer|as though + past modal (unreal comparison)]]. She addressed engineers, secretaries and strangers with the same warm, [[voc|weary|C1 vocabulary: tired, worn out]] self-assurance. Lucho, [[part|having spent his adolescence buried in textbooks rather than among people|Perfect participle clause (having + past participle)]], found her [[voc|mesmerising|C1 vocabulary: so fascinating you cannot look away]].
“You're very young,” she remarked, that first afternoon. “I'm twenty-five,” he replied, [[adv|as if the figure were some kind of defence|as if + subjunctive were (unreal comparison)]].
She laughed — not unkindly — and something inside him snapped shut, like a switch. Contact.
## Node 02 · No Reference — The first three months

[[cleft|What nobody at the office knew was that Lucho had never had a girlfriend.|Wh-cleft (What … was that)]] Not one. While his peers [[adv|had been learning how to argue, how to forgive and how to walk away|Past perfect continuous (had been + -ing)]], he had been studying how current behaves when it [[voc|encounters|C1 vocabulary: meets, comes up against]] resistance.
He had, in short, no [[voc|frame of reference|C1 collocation: a set of experiences used to judge something]]. Nothing to measure her against.

Within three months he was in love — or in whatever he had decided love must be. He [[voc|devoted himself|C1 vocabulary: devote oneself to = give all one's time and energy to]] to Carolina [[voc|wholeheartedly|C1 vocabulary: completely, without doubts]], with the [[voc|solemnity|C1 vocabulary: deep seriousness]] of a man wiring a hospital. If she called, he answered; if she sounded low, he cancelled whatever he had planned.

Carolina shared a house with her seventeen-year-old son — a house that, strictly speaking, belonged to a bank. She was [[voc|juggling|C1 vocabulary: managing several things with difficulty]] a mortgage, a car loan and three credit cards, and whenever money came up, she spoke of it the way people speak of the weather: as something that simply [[voc|befalls|C1 vocabulary (formal): happens to someone, usually something bad]] you.
“If I only ever paid the minimum, I'd never get to the end of it,” she once told him, laughing.
[[adv|He should have paid attention to the sentence rather than to the voice delivering it.|Past modal of criticism (should have + past participle)]]
## Node 03 · Heat, Then Fire — Year one
Her whims started [[voc|modestly|C1 vocabulary: in a small way]]: a dinner here, a weekend away there, a phone more recent than his own. Lucho paid, and paying felt like proof.

By the end of the first year, he had requested two advances on his salary and [[adv|had had his credit limit raised twice|Causative (have + object + past participle)]]. [[inv|Not only was he covering his own expenses, but he had also begun to cover hers.|Inversion after Not only … but also]] [[part|Though earning a respectable salary for his age|Reduced adverbial clause (Though + -ing)]], he ended every month [[voc|broke|Informal C1 vocabulary: with no money at all]].
He never referred to it as debt. He called it helping.

Electrical work has a rule: resistance generates heat, and heat, [[part|left unattended for long enough|Past participle clause (= if it is left unattended)]], generates fire. Lucho knew the rule [[voc|inside out|C1 idiom: completely, in every detail]]; he had explained it to technicians dozens of times. [[cleft|What he could not do was apply it to himself.|Wh-cleft (What … was + infinitive)]]
[[inv|Had somebody warned him, would he have listened?|Inverted third conditional in a question]] Probably not. Men in love make terrible engineers.
## Node 04 · The Lights Go Out Quietly — Manizales, Caldas
His parents were waiting in Manizales.

At first he [[adv|would visit|would + infinitive (past habit)]] them every month; then every other month; then he lost count. Weekends were expensive, Carolina needed him, the road was long. Each excuse was [[voc|plausible|C1 vocabulary: reasonable, easy to believe]] in isolation; together, they formed a wall.
His mother phoned; he answered less and less. His father's messages grew shorter each time, as though brevity might [[voc|conceal|C1 vocabulary (formal): hide]] his disappointment.
[[inv|Only when he finally looked at a calendar did he realise|Inversion after Only when … (did + subject)]] that more than a year had gone by without a single visit.

An open circuit is undramatic. Nothing explodes; nothing burns. The current simply stops arriving, and everything downstream goes dark — quietly, [[part|with nobody raising their voice|Absolute clause (with + noun + -ing)]].
He kept assuring himself that he would go home soon. Soon became a word he no longer trusted.
## Node 05 · What Distance Removes — Ibagué, Tolima · after almost two years
After almost two years, Lucho was transferred to Ibagué.
He told himself it was merely a change of address. “If we organise the weekends, we'll be fine,” he said, and he believed it.

[[part|Having spent two years adapting himself to her schedule, her moods and her emergencies|Perfect participle clause (Having + past participle)]], he had [[voc|all but|C1 vocabulary: almost completely]] forgotten how to spend a Sunday alone. His new flat was spotless, silent and unbearable. [[adv|He would rather have been exhausted than idle|would rather have + past participle]], so he worked late, rang her at eleven and counted the days.

Distance does not break a relationship on its own. [[cleft|What distance does is strip away the noise|Wh-cleft with do (What … does is + infinitive)]], and in the silence you finally hear what the relationship actually sounds like.
[[cleft|What Lucho heard, though he refused to name it, was static.|Wh-cleft + concessive clause (though)]]
## Node 06 · The Invoice — A Tuesday, over the phone
[[cleft|It was Carolina who ended it.|It-cleft (It was … who)]]

She did so on a Tuesday, over the phone, in the same [[voc|composed|C1 vocabulary: calm and in control]] voice she used for everything else. She said she needed her freedom; she said he deserved someone his own age; she said several things that sounded reasonable and explained nothing.
[[inv|No sooner had she finished than he was apologising|Inversion: No sooner … than]] — [[adv|though he could not have said what for|Past modal (could not have + past participle)]].
He hung up. Two years, an [[voc|inflated|C1 vocabulary: made bigger than it should be]] credit limit and a family he had stopped visiting: that was the invoice.

A fuse is designed to blow so that the rest of the system survives. Technically, then, he had been saved. He did not feel saved. He felt like a house at three in the morning, with everything switched off.
[[inv|Had he grasped, at twenty-five, what a whim really costs, his life would look entirely different today.|Mixed conditional with inversion (past condition → present result)]]
## Node 07 · A Second Circuit — Ibagué · a few weeks later
He did not wait. Within a few weeks he was seeing Silvia, a twenty-two-year-old who laughed easily and, initially at least, asked very few questions.
The relationship became physical almost at once, and for a while Lucho [[voc|mistook intensity for intimacy|C1 vocabulary: mistake A for B = confuse one thing with another]].

But something had been left behind in Buga: the patience, the small attentions, the absurd devotion. [[inv|Never again did any of it resurface.|Inversion after Never again (did + subject)]] He was affectionate, but efficiently so. Present, but not quite.
Silvia noticed. She had never met Carolina, yet she could sense her, the way you sense a wall in a darkened room.
“You treat me like an obligation,” she told him. “That's not true,” he said, and changed the subject — which is, of course, one way of admitting things.
She has threatened to leave him at least five times. [[inv|Not once has she packed a bag.|Inversion after Not once (has + subject)]]
## Node 08 · The Heat in the Wall — Now
Then, one night, she told him something [[adv|she had evidently been carrying around for weeks|Past perfect continuous]]: her ex-boyfriend had once come to the house.
Nothing had happened, she said — and it probably hadn't. [[cleft|What she did not explain was why she had kept quiet for so long.|Wh-cleft (What … was)]]

Lucho understood more than he [[voc|let on|C1 phrasal verb: let on = show or admit what you know]]. [[adv|He must have sensed it long before she confessed|Past modal of deduction (must have + past participle)]]; a man who has lived with silence learns its shape.

And yet he did nothing. He did not shout. He did not investigate. He did not leave. He simply carried on as usual, [[adv|as if the conversation had been a minor maintenance issue in an otherwise functioning system|as if + past perfect (unreal past)]].

Silvia is tired. Not angry — tired, which is far more [[voc|ominous|C1 vocabulary: suggesting that something bad will happen]]. Anger is current; exhaustion is a circuit [[part|already switched off|Reduced relative clause (past participle)]], waiting only for somebody to notice.
The system is still running. All the lights are on. [[inv|Only if you put your hand on the wall will you feel the heat.|Inversion after Only if (will + subject)]]

questions.q: Why does the narrator say Lucho had 'no frame of reference' when he met Carolina?
options: He had never been in a relationship to compare this one with.
He did not know anyone in Buga.
He had studied a different kind of engineering.
He could not understand Carolina's accent.
questions.explain_es: Node 02: 'What nobody at the office knew was that Lucho had never had a girlfriend… Nothing to measure her against.'

questions.q: Which heading best summarises Node 03?
questions.explain_es: Node 03 cuenta cómo Lucho pagó los caprichos de Carolina con adelantos de sueldo y más cupo de crédito: 'He never referred to it as debt.'

questions.q: Which heading best fits Node 05?
questions.explain_es: Node 05: la distancia 'strip[s] away the noise, and in the silence you finally hear what the relationship actually sounds like'.

questions.q: Lucho's salary was low for a man of his age.
questions.explain_es: Node 03: 'Though earning a respectable salary for his age, he ended every month broke.' El sueldo era bueno; el problema eran los gastos.

questions.q: Carolina's son disapproved of the relationship.
questions.explain_es: El texto solo dice que Carolina vivía con su hijo de diecisiete años; no menciona su opinión.

questions.q: Lucho's parents travelled to Buga to see him.
questions.explain_es: Node 04 dice que sus padres 'were waiting in Manizales' y que él dejó de visitarlos, pero no dice si ellos lo visitaron.

questions.q: What does the narrator imply with 'Men in love make terrible engineers'?
options: Love stops people from applying knowledge they already have.
Engineers are bad at relationships by nature.
Lucho lost his job because of Carolina.
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: Lucho 'knew the rule inside out', pero 'What he could not do was apply it to himself'.

questions.q: What can be inferred from 'and changed the subject — which is, of course, one way of admitting things'?
options: Silvia's accusation was at least partly true.
Lucho did not hear what Silvia said.
Lucho wanted to talk about Carolina.
questions.explain_es: Node 07: cambiar de tema es 'one way of admitting things', es decir, Lucho reconoce sin palabras que ella tiene razón.

questions.q: 'For a while Lucho mistook intensity for intimacy' means that he…
options: confused strong physical passion with real emotional closeness
was afraid of being close to Silvia
questions.explain_es: Mistake A for B = confundir A con B: creyó que la intensidad era intimidad.

questions.q: In Node 08, exhaustion is described as 'far more ominous' than anger. 'Ominous' is closest in meaning to…
options: threatening, a sign of something bad
questions.explain_es: 'Ominous' = de mal agüero: el cansancio de Silvia anuncia el final mejor que la rabia.

questions.q: Complete the inversion: "No sooner had she finished ____ he was apologising."
questions.explain_es: La estructura es No sooner + had + sujeto + participio … than: 'No sooner had she finished than he was apologising'.

questions.q: Rewrite with inversion: Silvia has not packed a bag once. → Not once ____
questions.explain_es: Tras 'Not once' al inicio, se invierte el auxiliar y el sujeto: 'Not once has she packed a bag.'

questions.q: Rewrite as an it-cleft to emphasise Carolina: Carolina ended it.
questions.answer: It was Carolina who ended it.
accept: It was Carolina who ended it
It was Carolina that ended it.
It was Carolina that ended it
questions.explain_es: It-cleft: It was + elemento enfatizado + who/that… 'It was Carolina who ended it.'

questions.q: What does the final image of the wall suggest about Lucho and Silvia's relationship?
options: It looks normal on the surface but is close to breaking down.
It is finally stable and safe.
Lucho is planning to go back to Carolina.
questions.explain_es: Node 08: 'All the lights are on. Only if you put your hand on the wall will you feel the heat' — todo parece funcionar, pero hay un problema oculto que se calienta.
